idiom_name: module privacy: private fields plus one checked method (a capability token can carry the right to call)
implementation_notes: Rust absorbs the pattern's first requirement into the language: privacy is checked by the compiler, everything is private by default, and pub(crate)/pub(in path) scope what may be reached from where, so a type that owns the resource and exposes only a mediating method cannot be bypassed from outside its module - attempts are compile errors, not discouragement. The runtime decision is still written by hand inside that method, where a zero-sized capability token (a type only the mediator or an authenticated subject can construct) can encode the right to perform an operation in the type system by being taken by value. The only escape hatches are unsafe code (transmutes, raw pointers, FFI) and over-broad visibility such as pub(crate) fields, so the review concentrates on the crate's privacy boundary and the unsafe blocks - which is what makes this the closest thing to a non-bypassable in-process mediator.
pitfalls: pub(crate) is not privacy against the rest of the crate: a sibling module can construct or mutate the resource through pub(crate) fields or a pub(crate) constructor and bypass the mediator.
Leaking a & or &mut to internal state (a getter, AsRef, Deref) hands out an unmediated reference; return guards, re-checking iterators or owned copies instead.
Deriving Clone, Default or Deserialize on the resource type gives callers unmediated construction paths - derive on the mediator's terms or not at all.
unsafe blocks, transmute and FFI can forge capabilities or alias the resource; every unsafe block in the mediator's dependency closure needs a justification, and the crate should fence unsafe off.
